_note: Single registry of every cited fact. status: verified = read by us at source or reliable summary; partial = real source, details to re-check; demo = our parameter. Never invent URLs.

sources.title: 5 Hazards of Human Spaceflight
sources.says: Five hazards: space radiation, isolation and confinement, distance from Earth, gravity fields, hostile/closed environments. Mars surface gravity is three-eighths of Earth's.

sources.title: Risks of Human Spaceflight
sources.says: Lists HRP risks (immune, sensorimotor, cardiovascular, decompression sickness, host-microorganism, hypoxia, nutrition, EVA injury, fitness, SANS, bone; behavioral, teamwork, sleep, systems support, dynamic loads; radiation-induced cancers). Spaceflight stress can reactivate dormant viruses causing rashes.

sources.title: Ongoing HRP Research in Space
sources.says: Artemis II investigations (ARCHeR, Immune Biomarkers, Standard Measures) and ISS studies (B-Complex, Brain Fluid Pressure, CIPHER, Thigh Cuff, Venous Haemostasis, Zero T2, Tempus Pro, etc.).

sources.title: Monitoring radiation for astronaut health (26 Feb 2026)
sources.says: Neutrons contribute about 30% of total radiation on the ISS; CANS active neutron spectrometer works continuously and autonomously.

sources.title: Why do we conduct science experiments in space?
sources.says: Deep-space missions mean more weightlessness, radiation, isolation, communication delay and less reliance on Earth; findings help with osteoporosis, cardiovascular disorders and Type-2 diabetes on Earth.

sources.title: International Space Station Guide — Systems (CHeCS)
sources.says: CHeCS comprises the Countermeasures System, Environmental Health System (air, microbes, water, acoustics, radiation) and Health Maintenance System.

sources.title: Biomedical Flight Controllers
sources.says: BME controllers are Mission Control's representatives for CHeCS, monitor bioenvironmental and environmental health data in real time, and work with the flight surgeon.

sources.title: Multifunctional Integrated Medical Devices
sources.says: ISS uses a collection of discrete medical devices to periodically assess crew health; NASA is evaluating a single integrated vital-sign monitoring system (Tempus Pro) for exploration.

sources.title: Tempus Pro (HRP investigation)
sources.says: Study of a commercial telemedicine device's ability to collect and integrate vital data, provide imaging and support near-real-time diagnosis.

sources.title: Tricorder Tech: Tempus Pro in space testing telemedicine capabilities
sources.says: In 2023 JSC chamber tests, novice users connected sensors and took vital signs easily with the iAssist step-by-step guidance.

sources.title: Biometric shirt for astronauts gets an Antarctic tryout
sources.says: CSA chief medical officer: misconception that astronauts are continuously monitored; vital signs are recorded mainly during exercise and spacewalks.

sources.title: Bio-Monitor: Keeping an eye on astronauts' vital signs
sources.says: Smart shirt plus tablet app; measures heart activity, blood pressure, breathing, SpO2, skin temperature, activity; data downlinked for analysis.

sources.title: Standard Measures (NASA Life Sciences Data Archive)
sources.says: Consistent core physiological, psychological and biological measurements of crews before, during and after flight; areas include behavioral health, biochemistry, bone, cardiovascular, immunology, muscle, ocular, sensorimotor.

sources.title: Overview of NASA Behavioral Health & Performance Standard Measures
sources.says: BHP Standard Measures include a neurocognitive battery, actigraphy, proximity sensors, cardiovascular monitors and mood/team self-reports.

sources.title: Cognition Test Battery (UPenn)
sources.says: 10-test battery developed for NASA, part of Standard Measures; includes a validated 3-minute PVT (PVT-B); used on ISS without reliable internet.

sources.title: Innovative software tools measure behavioral alertness (Spinoff 2013)
sources.says: PVT-B self test renamed Reaction Self-Test on ISS; informs astronauts when performance drops below optimal.

sources.title: Basner M, Mollicone D, Dinges DF. Validity and sensitivity of a brief psychomotor vigilance test (PVT-B) to total and partial sleep deprivation. Acta Astronautica 2011
sources.publisher: Acta Astronautica (author manuscript on PubMed Central)
sources.says: PVT-B: test shortened from 10 min to 3 min and inter-stimulus interval from 2-10 s to 1-4 s; lapse threshold lowered from 500 ms to 355 ms. Checked at source 14 Nov 2026 (some later papers describe the ISI as 2-5 s; the original paper says 1-4 s).

sources.title: Ocular surveillance in astronauts (NTRS 20170009173)
sources.says: On-orbit vision exam: distance acuity (Acuity Pro on laptop), near acuity (handheld card), Amsler grid (laptop), plus ultrasound, fundoscopy, OCT.

sources.title: The case for expanding visual assessments during spaceflight (Prehospital and Disaster Medicine)
sources.says: In-orbit functional vision assessment: static acuity, Amsler grid, self-report; 69% of US ISS crew had >20 um RNFL thickening in at least one eye on OCT.

sources.title: SANS and vision (Eye, 2024)
sources.says: Space Anticipation Glasses are kept aboard ISS to mitigate the hyperopic shift associated with SANS; in-flight testing includes acuity and Amsler grid.

sources.title: Ocular Health in ISS Crews (NTRS 20150003006)
sources.says: Research protocol in-flight tests on flight days 10, 30, 60, 90, 120 and R-30; computer-based visual tests include acuity, Amsler grid, contrast sensitivity and a questionnaire. Checked at source 14 Nov 2026.

sources.title: Actigraphy device for Artemis II human health study
sources.says: ARCHeR wrist device measures motion, sleep patterns and light exposure.

sources.title: NASA's Artemis 2 will test human health in deep space like never before
sources.says: ARCHeR wristbands support real-time health monitoring; each crew member carries a Crew Active Dosimeter; Orion has thousands of radiation sensors.

sources.title: Medical Data Architecture capabilities and design (NTRS 20170009788)
sources.says: Test Bed 1 automates collection of ECG, HR, skin temp, respiration, medications from Astroskin, ECG device and Dose Tracker into an EMR for the CMO; standalone operation.

sources.title: Crew Health and Performance Integrated Data System Platform (AsMA 2025)
sources.says: Back-end platform to acquire, process, store and distribute integrated crew health data for crew and ground; data currently spread across many systems; chest pain scenario.

sources.title: CHP-IDSP: Project Updates (HRP IWS 2025)
sources.says: Periodic Health Status exam data flows; CMO uses a personal computing device integrated with the vehicle's CHP-IDSP; Orion medical kit integration.

sources.title: The NASA Integrated Medical Model (IMM) overview
sources.says: Stochastic model of 100 spaceflight medical conditions; outputs total medical events, Crew Health Index (0-100%), resource use.

sources.title: Integrated Medical Model overview (NTRS 20150002713)
sources.says: Lists the 100 IMM medical conditions (47 have occurred, 53 possible).

sources.title: Lemery J, Easter B, Lehnhardt K. Earth Independent Medical Operations: Foundations to Advance Long Duration Mission Health (AsMA 2023 presentation)
sources.says: NASA Exploration Medical Capability (HRP) presentation, AsMA May 2023. Defines EIMO as the gradual transition of medical care and decision making from terrestrial to space-based assets. Exploration missions have no real-time communications and no evacuation; communication latency calls for on-board decision support and a higher on-board medical capability. Checked 14 Nov 2026 (PDF text).

sources.title: OCHMO-TB-004 Carbon Dioxide technical brief
sources.says: NASA-STD-3001 V2 6004: 1-hour average ppCO2 in habitable volume no more than 3 mmHg; headaches reported at 2.8-4.5 mmHg; fatigue/malaise above 4.5 mmHg.

sources.title: OCHMO-TB-004 Carbon Dioxide (web)
sources.says: To keep headache risk below 1%, 7-day average CO2 must stay below 2.5 mmHg; 0.5% CO2 = 3.8 mmHg; 3 mmHg limit keeps headache incidence below 1.4%.

sources.title: McCray M, Sturtz R. Using CFD to Predict Inspired CO2 and O2 after Ventilation Shutoff During a Gateway Emergency Response or Maintenance (ICES-2025-402)
sources.says: Uses time-limited ppCO2 exposure bands: up to nominal indefinite; nominal-6.8 mmHg 8 h; 6.8-10 mmHg 4 h; 10-15 mmHg 1 h (re-checked in the PDF 14 Nov 2026). The document does not say which requirement the bands come from, so the 6.8 mmHg ACT line stays a demo choice based on this source (the rule also cites SRC_DEMO_RULE_BANDS).

sources.title: OSHA Occupational Chemical Database: Carbon dioxide
sources.says: OSHA PEL (General Industry, 29 CFR 1910.1000 Table Z-1): 5,000 ppm (9,000 mg/m3) as an 8-hour TWA; NIOSH REL 5,000 ppm TWA with a 30,000 ppm STEL. Checked 14 Nov 2026. The 3.8 mmHg equivalent is from SRC_NASA_CO2_PAGE (0.5% CO2 = 3.8 mmHg), not from this page.

sources.title: OCHMO-TB-020 Design for Ionizing Radiation Protection
sources.says: V1 4030 career effective dose < 600 mSv (all ages and sexes); V1 4031 SPE design limit < 250 mSv; V1 4029 ALARA.

sources.title: OCHMO standards overview (Sept 2021)
sources.says: Career 600 mSv; SPE 250 mSv; GCR design target below 1.3 mSv/day in free space and 0.8 mSv/day on planetary surfaces.

sources.title: OCHMO-TB-002 ECLSS: Human-Centered Approach
sources.says: V2 6012 health limits 18 C/75% RH to 27 C/25% RH; V2 6013 performance zone 20-25 C and 30-60% RH; V2 6109 water at least 2.5 L/day per crewmember; V2 7003 average 3,035 kcal/day.

sources.title: Barger LK et al. Prevalence of sleep deficiency and use of hypnotic drugs in astronauts. Lancet Neurology 2014
sources.publisher: Brigham and Women's Hospital via ScienceDaily
sources.says: NASA schedules 8.5 h sleep; measured mean sleep was ~6.09 h on ISS missions (5.96 h shuttle).

sources.title: Risk of Spaceflight-Induced Bone Changes
sources.says: Bones lose 1-1.5% density per month on 4-6 month missions; exercise is essential.

sources.title: Astronaut Exercise (ISS research)
sources.says: ISS crew members average about two hours of exercise per day (schedules allot about 2.5 h including set-up).

sources.title: Sibonga JD, Pietrzyk R. Evidence Report: Risk of Renal Stone Formation (NASA HRP, 2017; NTRS 20170004709)
sources.says: Risk factors for stone formation in spaceflight include increased calcium excretion due to net bone resorption and low urine volume; urine analyses of crew showed hypercalciuria and reduced urine volumes. Checked 14 Nov 2026 (PDF text).

sources.title: Kunz H et al. Alterations in hematologic indices during long-duration spaceflight. BMC Hematology 2017
sources.says: 31 ISS astronauts: hematocrit was 12.2 %, 12.2 % and 10.0 % higher (relative) at early, mid and late flight than pre-flight; samples were analysed up to 48 h after collection and that delay alone raised hematocrit by about 4.7 % in ground controls, so part of the rise is an artefact. RBC and hemoglobin were also elevated; values returned to baseline within 30 days of landing. Checked 14 Nov 2026 (abstract and publisher summary).

sources.title: Stahn AC et al. Increased core body temperature in astronauts during long-duration space missions. Scientific Reports 2017
sources.says: Resting core body temperature on the ISS was about 1.0 C above pre-flight baseline, developing gradually over about 2.5 months; during exercise it rose higher and faster than on Earth. Measured with a non-invasive forehead sensor. Checked 14 Nov 2026. ARGUS applies no shift in the demo.

sources.title: NASA OSDR OSD-569 — Inspiration4 complete blood count
sources.says: Real CBC values for 4 anonymised commercial astronauts at L-92, L-44, L-3 and post-flight, with lab reference ranges (e.g., hematocrit 38.5-50% / 35-45%; WBC 3.8-10.8 x10^3/uL). No in-flight samples. File list (OSDR API, checked 14 Nov 2026): LSDS-7_Complete_Blood_Count_CBC.upload_SUBMITTED.csv and LSDS-7_Complete_Blood_Count_CBC_TRANSFORMED.csv.

sources.title: NASA OSDR OSD-575 — SpaceX Inspiration4 Blood Serum Metabolic Panel and Immune/Cardiac Cytokine Arrays
sources.says: Inspiration4 (3-day LEO mission, Sept 2021, four private astronauts): serum collected pre-flight (L-92, L-44, L-3) and post-flight (R+1, R+45, R+82); comprehensive metabolic panel by Quest Diagnostics plus cytokine panels (Eve Technologies, Alamar). The CMP file (LSDS-8_Comprehensive_Metabolic_Panel_CMP.upload_SUBMITTED.csv) has a glucose row per sample with lab reference range (e.g. 65-99 mg/dL). The study metadata does not record fasting state. Checked 14 Nov 2026 (OSDR API metadata and file).

sources.title: General adult vital-sign reference ranges (HR 60-100, SpO2 >=95%, temperature)
sources.says: MedlinePlus 'Vital signs' (url): adult resting pulse 60 to 100 beats per minute; temperature 97.7-99.1 F (36.5-37.3 C), average 98.6 F (37 C). MedlinePlus 'Pulse oximetry' (https://medlineplus.gov/lab-tests/pulse-oximetry/): normal oxygen saturation 95% to 100%; readings may be 2% to 4% off. Both checked 14 Nov 2026. ARGUS's own band edges (50-100 bpm nominal; the 90% SpO2 edge; 36.1-37.4 C nominal and the 35.0/37.5/38.0 C edges) are not stated on these pages; they are ARGUS demo band edges and cite SRC_DEMO_RULE_BANDS.

sources.title: Blood pressure categories (2017 ACC/AHA guideline, AHA patient page)
sources.says: Normal <120 and <80; elevated 120-129 and <80; stage 1 130-139 or 80-89; stage 2 >=140 or >=90; severe/crisis higher than 180 and/or higher than 120. Checked 14 Nov 2026.

sources.title: ADA Standards of Care — glucose categories
sources.says: Fasting plasma glucose 100-125 mg/dL prediabetes range; >=126 diabetes range; random >=200 with classic symptoms; 140-199 is the 2-hour tolerance-test range (not a random-sample category). Checked 14 Nov 2026. Hypoglycemia levels (<70, <54) not re-checked.

sources.title: Watson NF et al. Recommended Amount of Sleep for a Healthy Adult: A Joint Consensus Statement of the AASM and SRS. Sleep 2015
sources.says: Adults should sleep 7 or more hours per night on a regular basis to promote optimal health (adults aged 18 to 60). Checked 14 Nov 2026.

sources.title: Near acuity screening reference (20/40 ~ logMAR 0.3)
sources.publisher: Wikipedia (LogMAR chart); University of Iowa EyeRounds
sources.says: Equivalence confirmed: 20/40 (6/12) = 0.30 logMAR (Wikipedia 'LogMAR chart' table; also log10(40/20) = 0.301). 20/40 is used in US driver-licensing standards for distance acuity (EyeRounds 'Uniform vision standards for driving', https://eyerounds.org/article/uniform_vision_standards_for_driving.htm, checked 14 Nov 2026). No source opened states 20/40 as a NEAR-acuity screening cut-off, so ARGUS's 0.3 logMAR Earth line stays a demo choice. Stays partial.

sources.title: Dodgson NA. Variation and extrema of human interpupillary distance. Proc. SPIE 5291, Stereoscopic Displays and Virtual Reality Systems XI, 36-46 (2004)
sources.says: Abstract: mean adult IPD is around 63 mm; the vast majority of adults lie in 50-75 mm; 45-80 mm includes almost all adults. Bibliographic data checked via Crossref and abstract read via the Semantic Scholar/OpenAlex records of this DOI, 14 Nov 2026 (the SPIE page blocks automated access). Used only to estimate viewing distance.

sources.title: Alavi A et al. Real-time alerting system for COVID-19 and other stress events using wearable data. Nature Medicine 2022
sources.says: Online detectors (NightSignal, RHRAD, CuSum) compare resting HR to personal baseline (streaming median) with an alerting state machine.

sources.title: Mishra T et al. Pre-symptomatic detection of COVID-19 from smartwatch data. Nature Biomedical Engineering 2020
sources.says: Elevations in resting heart rate relative to the individual baseline detected 63% of cases before symptoms with a two-tier warning system.

sources.title: When 911 is millions of miles away: PSU researcher builds AI guardian for Mars missions
sources.says: NASA-funded AI health display learns each astronaut's physiology and updates the baseline during the mission.

sources.title: Wang W, den Brinker AC, Stuijk S, de Haan G. Algorithmic principles of remote PPG. IEEE TBME 64(7):1479-1491, 2017
sources.says: Introduces the POS (plane-orthogonal-to-skin) rPPG algorithm.

sources.title: Kossack et al. Automatic region-based heart rate measurement using rPPG (ICCV Workshops 2021)
sources.says: POS applied per facial ROI; POS reported best among traditional methods under varying lighting.

sources.title: MediaPipe Face Landmarker — Web guide
sources.says: Browser face landmark detection: 478 3D landmarks, 52 blendshapes, transformation matrix; VIDEO running mode; npm @mediapipe/tasks-vision.

sources.title: NOAA SWPC GOES proton flux products and JSON
sources.says: 5-minute integral proton flux; S-scale thresholds 10/100/1,000/10,000/100,000 pfu at >=10 MeV; >=100 MeV alert at 1 pfu; JSON at services.swpc.noaa.gov/json/goes/.

sources.title: NASA DONKI SEP web service
sources.says: Space weather event catalog incl. Solar Energetic Particle events; web service endpoints with startDate/endDate (default last 30 days).

sources.title: NOAA list of Solar Proton Events affecting the Earth environment
sources.says: Not needed for the build any more: when no event was captured, the replay uses the synthetic profile of doc 10 section 8 (SRC_DEMO_RADIATION_MODEL). NOAA states that it compiles such a list; its current URL was not located. Re-checked 14 Nov 2026: no code, seed file or handbook page cites this id, so nothing on screen rests on it.

sources.title: ISS dose-equivalent rate reported alongside the lunar-surface measurement (Zhang et al. 2020)
sources.says: For the same period as the Chang'E-4 measurement, the dose equivalent on board the ISS was 731 uSv/day (523 from galactic cosmic rays, 208 from the South Atlantic Anomaly). ARGUS uses 0.7 mSv/day. Checked 14 Nov 2026 (secondary report of the paper).

sources.title: NASA OSDR RadLab
sources.says: Single point of access to radiation telemetry data from multiple databases maintained by multiple space agencies: ISS (LEO) and beyond-LEO instruments, time series and absorbed-dose-rate maps. Checked 14 Nov 2026 (the page names no specific partner agency). Cited as the data portal for ISS dosimetry; the 0.7 mSv/day figure itself comes from SRC_ISS_DOSE.

sources.title: Zeitlin C et al. Measurements of energetic particle radiation in transit to Mars on the Mars Science Laboratory. Science 2013
sources.publisher: Science (value as reported by NASA JPL)
sources.says: RAD measured an average of about 1.8 mSv/day (1.84 in the paper) of GCR dose equivalent inside the MSL spacecraft during the cruise to Mars. Checked 14 Nov 2026 (NASA JPL release).

sources.title: Zhang S et al. First measurements of the radiation dose on the lunar surface. Science Advances 2020
sources.says: Average dose equivalent of 1,369 uSv/day (about 1.37 mSv/day) on the lunar surface (Chang'E-4 LND). Checked 14 Nov 2026 (paper front page and press summaries).

sources.title: Hassler DM et al. Mars' surface radiation environment measured with the MSL Curiosity rover. Science 2014
sources.publisher: Science (value as quoted in J. Space Weather Space Clim. 2016)
sources.says: Average GCR dose equivalent rate of 0.64 +/- 0.12 mSv/day on the Martian surface (MSL RAD). Checked 14 Nov 2026 (quoted value).

sources.title: HRA 3D Reference Library (HuBMAP) / NIH 3D Body, Male & Female
sources.says: Visible Human male/female united body sets and organs as GLB, CC BY 4.0 (NIH 3D entries 3DPX-021022 male, 3DPX-021627 female).

sources.title: BodyParts3D, The Database Center for Life Science
sources.says: Licensed under CC BY 4.0 since 2025-02-27 (license page checked 14 Nov 2026). Required credit: "BodyParts3D, (c) The Database Center for Life Science licensed under CC Attribution 4.0 International". Older releases and OBJ file comments still mention CC BY-SA 2.1 Japan.

sources.title: NASA Space Apps Project Submission Guide
sources.says: Demo: video <=30 s or <=7 slides, English, public link; NASA data required for global awards; criteria: Impact, Creativity, Validity, Relevance, Presentation. Note 14 Nov 2026: when re-opened, this page still showed last year's dates; the 2026 dates (submission opens Sat 14 Nov 09:00, closes Sun 15 Nov 23:59 local time) are on https://www.spaceappschallenge.org/2026/. Re-read the 2026 guide (released 13 Nov) before submitting.

sources.title: ARGUS demo parameters: rule band edges
sources.says: Band edges marked [demo] in docs/07_CLINICAL_RULES.md are our own choices for this prototype; they are not clinical or NASA limits.

sources.title: ARGUS demo parameters: personal baseline engine
sources.says: CuSum k = 0.5, thresholds z 2.0/3.0 and S 4.0/8.0, drift 2.5, hysteresis 1.5, recovery reset, sigma floors and the -0.9 h expected sleep shift (docs/08_BASELINE_ENGINE.md) are tuning choices for this prototype.

sources.title: ARGUS demo parameters: radiation model and shelter policy
sources.says: K = 0.05 mSv/h per pfu, shield factors, dose verdict thresholds (80 %, 95 %, 125 mSv), the shelter policy table and the synthetic S2 replay profile (docs/10_RADIATION.md) are illustrative; real crew dose comes from dosimeters and real shelter calls from radiation specialists.

sources.title: ARGUS demo parameters: measurement quality and staleness
sources.says: rPPG quality thresholds, staleness multipliers (1.5x and 3x cadence), assumed webcam field of view and similar measurement settings (docs/09_MEASUREMENT_LAB.md, docs/04_REQUIREMENTS.md) are our own choices.

sources.title: ARGUS demo parameters: readiness index and gamification
sources.says: The readiness formula, points, streaks and badges (docs/11_UI_UX_SPEC.md section 9) are a demo index, not an Integrated Medical Model output.

sources.title: ARGUS demo parameters: simulated crew, scenarios and mission profile assumptions
sources.says: Crew baselines, noise, scenarios, pre-mission career doses and the Mars-transit delay table (seed/crew.json, seed/scenarios.json, seed/missions.json) are simulated or assumed and are labeled as such.
